title: The Impact of Health Care Reform on Hospital and Preventive Care: Evidence from Massachusetts
research_question: Does achieving near-universal health insurance coverage for an entire state population affect the level and composition of insurance coverage, hospital utilization patterns (such as length of stay and emergency-room admissions), use of preventive care, patient safety, and hospital costs? How are these effects distributed across age, gender, income, and race subgroups?
data_description: The analysis draws on three main data sources covering 2004–2008/2009. The primary dataset is the Healthcare Cost and Utilization Project (HCUP) Nationwide Inpatient Sample (NIS), a stratified 20% nationally representative sample of U.S. community hospitals containing the universe of discharges (regardless of payer) for sampled hospitals, totaling about 36 million discharges from 3,090 hospitals across 42 states (48 in Massachusetts). The unit of observation is the hospital discharge, with quarterly timing. Key variables include primary payer (uninsured, Medicaid, private, Medicare, CommCare/other), length of stay, emergency-room source of admission, AHRQ Prevention Quality Indicators, Patient Safety Indicators, Inpatient and Pediatric Quality Indicators, and hospital-level all-payer cost-to-charge ratios. Population-level coverage is measured using the March Current Population Survey (2004–2009), and outpatient/preventive care behaviors come from the Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System (2004–2009, ~2.3 million observations).
institutional_context: In April 2006, Massachusetts enacted Chapter 58, sweeping legislation aimed at near-universal health insurance coverage. Core provisions included an individual mandate to obtain coverage (effective July 2007) with tax penalties, an employer mandate for firms with more than 10 full-time employees, expansions of Medicaid (MassHealth) including raising children's eligibility to 300% of poverty and restoring benefits to populations cut during the 2002–2003 fiscal crisis, and creation of CommCare, offering free coverage up to 150% of poverty and subsidized coverage up to 300% of poverty. A new state-run exchange (the Connector) offered regulated bronze/silver/gold CommChoice plans and Young Adult plans, merged the individual and small-group markets, maintained community rating, and required dependent coverage to age 26. The reform's rollout was staggered: Medicaid expansions took effect almost immediately, while the individual mandate and full implementation came in mid-2007. The reform closely prefigures the March 2010 federal health reform, making it a uniquely informative setting for assessing population-wide coverage expansion.
